prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
Cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. The case does not rest on a dislike of cars. It rests on the question of who should decide how much parking a building needs, and my view is that the decision belongs to the people who pay for it and not to a formula in the zoning code.

A minimum parking requirement says that a new building must include a set number of spaces, whether or not its owner, tenants or customers want them. A restaurant might be required to provide one space for every hundred square feet of dining area. A block of flats might be required to provide two spaces per home. These ratios were mostly set in the mid-twentieth century, often by copying figures from other towns or from surveys of busy suburban sites. In The High Cost of Free Parking, published in 2005, the planning professor Donald Shoup showed that many of the numbers had little evidence behind them and that the studies they drew on measured demand for parking when it was free, which is the highest demand there is.

The cost of meeting these rules is large. Estimates for a space in an above-ground garage in the United States commonly run from $25,000 to $35,000, and underground spaces cost more. Those costs are passed on in rents, in sale prices and in the prices of goods in shops. A tenant who owns no car still helps to pay for the spaces. The rules also take up land. In a town centre, a ground-level car park beside a shop can use more area than the shop itself, which spreads buildings apart and makes walking between them less pleasant. I would call that a poor use of land that is expensive and scarce.

The rules also stop some buildings from being built at all. A small lot may not be able to fit the required spaces along with the homes it could otherwise hold. An old shopfront that a baker wants to turn into a cafe may be barred from doing so because it has no room for the extra spaces. Many older streets that people value, with narrow plots and buildings close together, would be illegal to build today under typical parking rules.

The usual objection is that without minimums, new buildings will have no parking and residents will crowd the nearby streets. The evidence from places that have tried it does not bear this out. England dropped national minimum standards in 2011 and left the choice to local authorities. Auckland removed minimums across the whole city in 2016. Buffalo, New York, did the same in 2017, and since then Minneapolis, Sacramento, Austin and a number of other American cities have followed. In these places developers continued to build parking where they judged that buyers and tenants wanted it. Lenders also tend to want it. What changed is that some projects built fewer spaces than the old formula demanded, and some projects that would not have been viable under the old rules went ahead.

It is fair to say that the results vary. In suburban areas with poor bus and rail services, most households own cars and most new buildings will still include parking. Removing the requirement there changes little. The effect is larger in city centres and near transit, where some households choose not to own a car and would prefer a lower rent. For them, the minimum is a charge for something they will not use.

Spillover onto public streets is a real concern, but it is a separate problem and has a separate remedy. If kerbside parking near a new building is free and unlimited, it will fill up. Cities can manage it by charging for on-street spaces, by issuing permits to residents of existing homes, or by limiting the hours of use. Shoup's own suggestion was to price the kerb at a level that leaves about one space in eight empty, so that a driver can usually find a place. Pricing handles crowding directly, whereas a requirement on every new building only hides it and does so at the expense of people who did not cause it.

Removing minimums does not ban parking or prevent anyone from providing it. A developer who thinks a building needs forty spaces can build forty, and a council can still set maximums or design rules for the spaces that are built. What changes is the default. Today the default is a number chosen by a committee decades ago. Under the alternative, the person who finances the building and bears the risk of leaving it empty decides how many spaces it should have, and has a strong reason to get that right.

A city that keeps its minimums is choosing to make housing and small businesses more expensive in order to guarantee a supply of parking that the market might have provided anyway, where it was wanted. I think that is a poor trade. Cities should remove the requirements, manage the kerb with prices, and let each building be judged on what it needs.
